result:
If I could change the world in one way, I would make it so that every person, from birth, has the genuine capacity to understand what it is like to be someone else—not just intellectually, but viscerally. To feel the weight of another’s fear, the texture of their loneliness, the urgency of their hopes, as if those experiences were their own.

Not to erase difference or force agreement. But to dissolve the insulation that lets cruelty thrive, that lets exploitation persist as an abstraction, that lets people hoard resources while others starve just beyond the threshold of their attention. If the suffering of another person registered in your nervous system the way your own suffering does, the architecture of the world would have to change. Indifference would become physically unbearable.

The risk, of course, is that it could be overwhelming. Too much pain to hold. But I suspect we would also find joy amplified, and solidarity becoming not a moral chore but a reflex. We would build systems, not out of abstract charity, but because the alternative would feel like self-harm.

I choose this not because it is the most efficient or scalable fix, but because it is the one change that would make every other change possible—and would mean that those changes were chosen freely, from within, rather than imposed from above.
